text: Stamford Bridge. The ninety-third minute. Barcelona are going out of the Champions League.
They haven't had a single shot on target all night. And then the ball rolls to Andrés Iniesta, just outside the penalty area.
It takes about a second for the ball to travel from his foot to the net. In this video, we're going to look at that one second from ten different angles.
By the end, you'll never see this goal the same way again.
Three angles on how Barça got here. Two on the chaos that surrounded the game. Three on the goal itself.
And two on what that one shot changed — for the club, and for football.
Angle one. The season.
This was Pep Guardiola's first season as coach, and his team had played some of the most beautiful football Europe had ever seen.
Just four days earlier, they had beaten Real Madrid six–two at the Bernabéu to all but win the league.
Now they were at Stamford Bridge, one game from a Champions League final. The league, the cup and Europe were all still possible. Nobody in Spain had ever won all three in one season.
Angle two. The first leg.
A week earlier, at the Camp Nou, Chelsea had done something almost nobody managed against Guardiola's team. They had stopped them from playing.
Chelsea defended deep, closed every gap, and left with a nil–nil draw.
It meant the second leg had one simple rule. If Barça scored even once at Stamford Bridge, Chelsea would need to score twice. Away goals counted double in a tie.
Angle three. The ninth minute.
It took Chelsea nine minutes to score. Michael Essien met a loose ball outside the area and hit a volley that flew in off the crossbar.
Now Barcelona needed a goal. And Chelsea, ahead and at home, could defend the way they had in the first leg.
For the next eighty minutes, Barça had the ball — and almost nothing to show for it.
Angle four. The red card.
In the sixty-sixth minute, it got worse. Éric Abidal was sent off after a challenge with Nicolas Anelka outside the box. Replays suggested there was barely any contact.
Barcelona were now a goal down, with ten men, away from home, with twenty-five minutes left.
Their passing game, built on having more players than the opponent around the ball, suddenly had one player fewer.
Angle five. The referee.
This is the part Chelsea supporters will never forget. Throughout the night, the Norwegian referee, Tom Henning Øvrebø, turned down a series of Chelsea penalty appeals.
One of the strongest was a handball by Gerard Piqué in the second half.
Years later, Øvrebø admitted that Chelsea should have been given at least one penalty.

It's an important angle, because it means the goal we're about to watch did not happen in a vacuum. To many people in London, Barcelona's moment of glory will always be a night of injustice. Both things can be true.
Angle six. The pass.
It starts with a cross from the right. Dani Alves sends the ball into the box. It's half-cleared.
The ball bounces to Lionel Messi on the edge of the area. Three Chelsea players close in on him immediately.
And Messi, who could have tried to shoot, does something simpler. He rolls it a few metres to his left. To Iniesta.
Angle seven. The strike.
Iniesta was not known as a goalscorer. He was a passer, a dribbler, the player who made everything around him easier.
He doesn't take a touch. He hits it first time, with the outside of his right foot curling it away from the goalkeeper — high, into the top corner.
From the edge of the area, about twenty metres out, a well-struck shot like that reaches the goal in roughly a second. Petr Čech barely has time to move.
One–one. On aggregate, one–one. But Barcelona had scored away from home. And that meant they were going through.
Angle eight. The touchline.
Watch the bench in that moment and you see something that tells you everything about that team.
Pep Guardiola, normally composed in his grey suit, sprinted down the touchline, arms in the air, with his staff and substitutes chasing behind him.
Iniesta tore off his shirt and disappeared under a pile of teammates. Victor Valdés ran the length of the pitch to join them.
There were still a few minutes to play. Chelsea threw everything forward. There was one more penalty appeal. Then the final whistle.
Angle nine. The fury.
The scenes at the final whistle were ugly. Chelsea players surrounded the referee. Michael Ballack chased him across the pitch.
Didier Drogba, who had already been substituted, marched onto the pitch and shouted his anger straight into the television cameras.
Øvrebø later said he received threatening messages for years afterwards. However you see the refereeing that night, no official deserves that.
For Barcelona, though, there was only one thing that mattered. They were going to Rome.
Angle ten. What it changed.
Without that shot, Barça are out. No final in Rome. No treble.
Instead, they won the Copa del Rey a week later, and confirmed the league title soon after.
On the twenty-seventh of May, in Rome, they beat Manchester United two–nil to become champions of Europe.
By the end of the year they had won six trophies out of six — the first team in history to do it.
And it might never have happened without one swing of Andrés Iniesta's right foot, in the ninety-third minute, from his team's first shot on target.
A year later, in the World Cup final in Johannesburg, Iniesta scored again — the extra-time winner that made Spain world champions for the first time.
Iniesta was never a prolific goalscorer. But when the biggest moments came, it was so often his foot the ball fell to.
He later called the Stamford Bridge goal one of the best memories of his life. For millions of Barça supporters, it's one of theirs too.
